source: In the 1950s, only a few sci-fi films and shows took place in the future, like the Fire Maidens of Outer Space (1956) which is a film about astronauts landing on one of Jupiter’s moons. For the most part, these stories were set in the audience’s present day – so, the 1950s.
claim: Among 1950s stories, 12.0% are set in the future, 78.0% in the present, 7.5% in the past and 2.5% in multiple/other settings.

source: In these 1950s stories, the world is often upended by an existential threat .
claim: In the 1950s, 72.5% of stories present an existential threat (answered “yes” or “somewhat”).

source: But in the majority of films, the protagonists figure it out – and leave the world better than the beginning of the story.
claim: In the 1950s, 76.5% of stories leave the world in a better place.

source: There’s been a steady increase in sci-fi stories that take place in the future
claim: The share of stories set in the future rises from 12.0% in the 1950s to 27.5% in the 2020s, reaching 29.5% in the 2010s.

source: The stakes are still the same as before; these sci-fi stories still present existential threats .
claim: The share presenting an existential threat ranges from 65.0% in the 1990s to 77.0% in the 2020s, and is 72.5% in the 1950s.

source: But we’re now more likely to face these existential threats in a dystopian or post-apocalyptic world
claim: The share of stories set in a dystopian or post-apocalyptic world rises from 10.5% in the 1950s to 45.5% in the 2020s.

source: This dystopian society is more likely to be marked by inequality – gaps in opportunity, wealth, and basic rights.
claim: The share of settings marked by inequality rises from 14.5% in the 1950s to 62.0% in the 2020s.

source: This often leads to a world marked by great amounts of suffering .
claim: The share of settings marked by suffering rises from 18.5% in the 1950s to 66.5% in the 2020s.

source: And increasingly, sci-fi stories depict militarized societies – although we might be seeing that trend turn around this decade.
claim: The share marked by a militarized society rises from 19.5% in the 1950s to 52.0% in the 2010s, then falls to 40.5% in the 2020s.

source: But these days, it’s much more likely that protagonists also have to overcome societal forces – political movements, systemic inequality, rampant capitalism.
claim: The share of stories where protagonists fight society rises from 19.5% in the 1950s to 68.5% in the 2010s and 2020s.

source: It’s also far more likely that the narrative explores inner conflicts – moral dilemmas, identity crises, and wrestling with our understanding of what it means to be human.
claim: The share of stories where protagonists battle with themselves rises from 26.0% in the 1950s to 82.0% in the 2010s and 2020s.

source: Ultimately, today’s sci-fi stories are far more likely to be a commentary on current social issues .
claim: The share of stories seen as a commentary on current social issues rises from 67.5% in the 1950s to 90.5% in the 2020s, peaking at 93.0% in the 2010s.

source: But even though the narrative arc starts us off in a terrible place, the protagonists make the world better over the course of the story.
claim: The share of stories whose characters make the world better is 76.5% in the 1950s, 86.5% in the 2010s and 84.5% in the 2020s.
